subject: B362A06F749D49B8A9B4080391A83C2E
introduction: This guide collects what ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, and Bahá’u’lláh’s secretary before Him, wrote to believers about books: encouragement to authors and translators, care that printed texts agree with reliable originals, instructions to copy and circulate letters, the rule that nothing concerning the Faith be printed without review and, in Persia, without the government’s leave, and replies to hostile or mistaken accounts. Scripture has its own book-history beside it: Hezekiah’s scribes, Baruch rewriting the burned scroll, Paul’s signature as “the token in every epistle” and his warning against letters “as from us”, Luke’s preface, the translators’ prefaces to Sirach and the King James Bible. The principle of review meets its classic opponents in Milton’s Areopagitica, Jefferson and Mill, who are placed here in contrast; Proverbs and Mill on hearing the other side bear on the polemical readings at the end.
questions: What are the reasons these readings give for reviewing a book before it is printed? Which are about accuracy, which about protection, and which about timing?
Milton trusts truth to win in an open contest. What is the case for a religious community reviewing what is published about its teachings, and what are the costs?
Reading 3 forbids publishing anything that injures feelings. Can a publication be both truthful about disagreements and obedient to that rule?
The readings care greatly about exact texts and faithful translation. Why does a religion of the book need that care, and what did earlier scriptures suffer for want of it?
Reading 186 faults a scholar for hearing one side only. How should a believer read histories written by critics?

outside.why: A collection of talks to be published, and the question of fidelity to what was said. Thucydides on the speeches in his history: it was in all cases difficult to carry them word for word in one’s memory.
He wished to make the corrections Himself. It seemed good to me also, having had perfect understanding of all things from the very first, to write unto thee in order.
A Bahá’í publication must never provoke or injure anyone’s feelings. Let your speech be always with grace, seasoned with salt.

Milton would have a press free even to offend: though all the winds of doctrine were let loose to play upon the earth, so Truth be in the field, we do injuriously, by licensing and prohibiting, to misdoubt her strength. Let her and Falsehood grapple. What does a religious community’s own press owe to that principle, and what to reading 3?
A library established and its books announced. Nehemiah, founding a library, gathered together the acts of the kings, and the prophets.
If two printed versions differ in meaning, inquire. Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it.
An unsigned letter, and how to know it authentic. Paul: the salutation of Paul with mine own hand, which is the token in every epistle: so I write.
Compare the text with a trusted scribe’s copy. These are also proverbs of Solomon, which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied out.
One jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law.
The friends’ histories contradict one another; gather them all. He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him.
A history read section by section at midnight. Bacon: read not to contradict and confute, nor to believe and take for granted, but to weigh and consider.
A book rendered into Arabic and read through carefully. Translation it is that openeth the window, to let in the light.
Translated pages to be reviewed before they go out. The same things uttered in Hebrew, and translated into another tongue, have not the same force in them.
She should correct the book. A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver.
A magazine that gladdens the friends. As cold waters to a thirsty soul, so is good news from a far country.
Thanks for a fair and truthful article. Buy the truth, and sell it not.
“He has written many books in this Cause.” Of making many books there is no end; and much study is a weariness of the flesh. What decides which books a community needs?
A book the friends are reading and praising. My tongue is the pen of a ready writer.
“Write the book which she had in mind.” Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it.
Talks translated with great labour. We do hear them speak in our tongues the wonderful works of God.
Books and pamphlets to be translated into many languages. Go ye therefore, and teach all nations.
Writings presented to a national library. A good book is the precious life-blood of a master spirit, embalmed and treasured up on purpose to a life beyond life.
Letters beautifully printed in fine handwriting. John preferred not to write: I would not write with paper and ink; I trust to come unto you, and speak face to face.
Letters received and read with joy. Ye are our epistle written in our hearts, known and read of all men.
Carry some copies and deliver them. Bring with thee the books, but especially the parchments.
A Tablet written to be printed. Now go, write it before them in a table, and note it in a book, that it may be for the time to come.
Copy this letter in forty or fifty copies and send them out. Baruch wrote again all the words of the book which the king had burned; and there were added besides unto them many like words.

“Unconfirmed publications are absolutely not permitted.” Jefferson: error of opinion may be tolerated where reason is left free to combat it. The readings concern what is published in the Faith’s name and with its texts. Does that difference answer Jefferson?

No book on the Cause may be printed without permission from the Centre of the Covenant. Mill: all silencing of discussion is an assumption of infallibility. What reasons do readings 156 to 165 give for review, and which of them would Mill accept?
Books need the permission of the government. Render therefore to all their dues.
To publish without the sovereign’s leave is to oppose the divine text. Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers.
Printing depends on consultation, and wisdom now counsels against it. Every purpose is established by counsel.
A compilation is good; its publication is not yet permitted. Jesus too imposed silences: see thou say nothing to any man.
Take a copy and destroy the originals. Seal up those things which the seven thunders uttered, and write them not.
A letter without the seal is meant to sow doubt. Be not soon shaken in mind, neither by word, nor by letter as from us.
A European’s book that does not conform to reality. Thou shalt not raise a false report.
An orientalist who met only one party’s followers. Mill: he who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that. The reading applies the rule to a scholar. To whom else does it apply?
“This is enough proof that what he hath written is spurious.” Believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God.
A history declared a fabrication from its own contents. If the thing follow not, nor come to pass, that is the thing which the Lord hath not spoken.
A scholar is writing a response. Be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness.
A newspaper account with many errors and some truth. Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.

shortfall: Most of the hundred readings are brief practical notes: thanks for a book or translation, instructions to print, copy, send or withhold a text. Companions were given to the principles among them (fidelity, translation, review, authenticity, polemic) and the notes themselves were mostly left alone.
